I've thought of a few things:

The Good

  • Software installation would be much safer due to the repo system
  • No one would have to go to every program individually to update them
  • Login passwords would most likely be required thus increasing security
  • Finding drivers would be a much simpler process due to the repo system

The Bad

  • It is possible every PC manufacturer would end up creating their own distros (HP Linux, Dell Linux, Acer Linux etc.)
  • Every single one will probably look different and the different companies will use the freedom they have to make a custom UI which can end up badly
  • Every distro would have its own repo which would mean whichever PC you buy also decides which software you can get immediately without adding extra repos
  • Software from large corps would have to either be released to every distros' repo or give users the option to add the repo for the software

This is just speculations, but I think with the way Linux is at the moment, there would be much fragmentation if every PC manufacturer literally created their own distros instead of basing theirs on another like Debian or RedHat, which would reduce the fragmentation a little bit, if they did that instead.
If history turned out different and Linux became the primary OS for PCs in its current form, what would end up going wrong or right?

The kernel would be full of proprietary code because hardware vendor won't open source their drivers. The kernel would become some kind of hybrid (module loading) just to try to mitigate this trend.

Oh wait, it is already happening.

Each PC manufacturer would almost definitely base their distro on a popular existing major distro, and would likely just add their own repo to the default repos for that distro. Limiting user access to standard repos would be corporate suicide in such an environment. Essentially, I would see it playing out very similarly to Android, in that respect.

They'd probably all use the default DE for whatever major distro they were basing it on as well, for brand recognition, which would be supported by minimal changes to the distro itself. There is a huge buyer gravitation towards the familiar which would all but ensure this level of standardization.
